Query: We still carry legacy exposure to Gammon India. Pull together every credit-risk event and red flag in this year's report - lender actions, payment defaults, auditor concerns, market and governance fallout - and tell me how serious the situation really is.

How entangled is Inox Wind with its promoter group and subsidiaries - through orders, funding, guarantees and settlements - and what does that mean for a lender to Inox Wind itself?

CEAT closed a sizeable overseas acquisition and stepped up capex this year. How has that changed its leverage, liquidity and debt-servicing capacity, and why did the rating agencies remain comfortable?

CEAT runs with current liabilities well above current assets. Is that a genuine short-term liquidity risk or a feature of its business model? Use the working-capital, funding and cash-flow evidence in the report.
Run a credit red-flag review on Refex Industries for this year. Which events, disclosures and balance-sheet features should worry a lender, and how do they net out against the rating it holds?
How much of Refex Industries' balance sheet and off-balance-sheet commitments is now tied up in its own group entities, and how did that change over the year?
Refex has been reshaping its business portfolio. What has it exited, what is it leaning into, and how does the shift change the risk profile of its revenue and receivables?

How has Banque Saudi Fransi's funding and liquidity position evolved over the year, and is it more or less resilient than a year ago? Consider deposit mix, wholesale funding and the regulatory liquidity measures.
Is Banque Saudi Fransi's loan book getting riskier even though its impairment charge fell? Walk through the growth mix, problem loans, coverage and provisioning.

How did Banque Saudi Fransi build its capital position this year, and how much of the improvement relies on hybrid and subordinated instruments rather than retained earnings? Flag anything inconsistent in how the ratios are presented.
Has Aldar's leverage and liquidity genuinely improved over the year, or does it just look better because of cash on hand? Assess its debt structure, funding sources and headroom.
How exposed is Aldar to its own customers and counterparties, and is it provisioning enough given how its receivables are ageing?
Metal Coatings' debt-service metrics swing wildly between its last two annual reports. Explain what actually drove that, and whether its underlying ability to service debt improved or weakened.
Trace Metal Coatings' dealings with its promoters and promoter-linked businesses across the FY2025 and FY2026 reports. What exposures existed, what changed, and are the disclosures consistent?
Looking at Metal Coatings' FY2026 balance sheet against FY2025, is liquidity getting tighter? Explain where cash has been absorbed and how it was funded.

If you had to re-underwrite Metal Coatings today using both of its last two annual reports, would your view of its creditworthiness change? Weigh the external rating, audit outcomes, earnings trend, related-party reliance and balance-sheet strength.

Bhadora Industries listed on the SME platform after a year of rapid growth. From a lender's perspective, how is that growth being financed and what do the quality of its receivables and working capital look like?
How reliable is the financial information Bhadora Industries gives its lenders and shareholders? Look for internal inconsistencies across the directors' report, auditor annexures and the notes.
GRM Overseas' sales fell this year but its receivables did not. How worried should a lender be about collections and liquidity, and does the company's own credit-loss accounting reflect the risk?
Infosys returned more cash to shareholders this year than it generated. Does that weaken its credit standing in any meaningful way? Look at liquidity, policy commitments and any one-off items.

Line up CEAT, Inox Wind, Refex, GRM Overseas and Metal Coatings on leverage, short-term liquidity and debt-servicing capacity using their latest reports. Which would you be most and least comfortable lending to over a one-year horizon, and why?

Across the Indian industrial companies in this set, whose receivables look most likely to turn into credit losses? Compare collection trends, ageing, concentration and how much each has actually provided.

Compare how exposed Refex, Inox Wind, Metal Coatings and GRM Overseas are to related parties - loans, guarantees, sales and receivables. Who carries the biggest group-contagion risk relative to its size?

Several of these companies recently raised, or tried to raise, equity from promoters and investors. What do those equity events - and how they ended - tell a credit analyst about sponsor support at Inox Wind, Refex, GRM Overseas and Bhadora?

Which companies faced legal, tax or regulatory actions this year that a credit committee should know about, and how material are they relative to each company's financial position? Compare Refex, Gammon India and Infosys.

Compare the external credit ratings of CEAT, Inox Wind, Refex and Metal Coatings with what their own financial statements show. Where does a rating look generous or conservative, and what would you watch?
Compare how Banque Saudi Fransi and Aldar fund themselves and manage liquidity risk. Which is more exposed to a funding-market shock, and what buffers does each hold?
Compare how Banque Saudi Fransi and Aldar measure and provision for expected credit losses. Whose provisioning looks more conservative relative to its problem exposures?

Compare how risk management is governed at board level at Infosys, CEAT, Banque Saudi Fransi and Aldar - who owns it, how independent the risk function is, and how actively the board engages. Which setup looks weakest?
Which rating agency rates Refex Industries' bank facilities, and what long-term rating did it reaffirm?
What was Banque Saudi Fransi's NPL coverage ratio at the end of 2025?
Who chairs the Risk Management Committee of Infosys?
What net profit did Aldar report for full-year 2025 in its 2025 annual report, and how did it compare with 2024?
Under the Basel Committee's original December 2017 timetable, what calibration did the output floor have from 1 January 2025?
What individual stress capital buffer did the Fed assign to each US GSIB for the 2025-26 cycle, according to these capital proposals?

We are a mid-sized lender that has only ever reserved for loan losses once they looked probable. Under the US lifetime expected-loss standard, what actually changes for us - in the timing of provisions, the information we must use, our equity and regulatory capital, and the data we need to keep - and why did standard-setters decide the old approach was inadequate?

If our bank were building its first lifetime-loss allowance process from scratch, what are the main building blocks we must decide, in what order, and at each step what evidence would a federal examiner expect to see before accepting the final number?

How does the US lifetime-loss allowance model differ from the international expected-loss model most non-US banks apply, why did the two standard-setters fail to agree on one approach, and what practical differences would a group reporting under both have to manage?

Our credit metrics have improved for three years, yet economists expect a downturn and we recently loosened underwriting on one product. How should management adjustments layered on the modelled allowance be designed, sized and documented so they neither miss these risks nor double count them, and what would make an examiner push back?

Our stress-testing team proposes reusing its nine-quarter supervisory scenarios and horizon as the allowance forecast and then snapping straight back to long-run averages. Is that acceptable? Explain what judgement the rules leave to management on the forecast window and the transition back to history, what is considered inappropriate, and how much of the allowance can end up depending on the post-forecast period.

We plan to license a vendor loss-forecasting model and also adapt our in-house stress-testing models for the credit-loss allowance. As the model-risk owner, what validation, monitoring and third-party oversight do supervisors expect, and what are the known limits of back-testing an allowance model?

A commercial borrower is in trouble and we now expect to be repaid from the property rather than the business. How do accounting rules and bank regulatory reporting differ in measuring the loss on such a loan, what happens when the property value later rises or falls, and how do we decide whether a loan qualifies in the first place?

How has the treatment of loan modifications for struggling borrowers changed in the US allowance framework over the past few years - comparing the early implementation guidance and the 2021 examiner handbook with the 2023 revised supervisory statement and current accounting guidance - and what does it mean for how a bank sets loan lives, measures losses and discloses modified loans?

Treasury wants to carry no credit-loss allowance at all on our government bonds, cash-secured loans and the guaranteed portions of government-backed loans. Under what conditions is a zero expected loss defensible, where do supervisors add extra conditions or comfort, and why can't strong collateral value alone justify zero?

For a large credit-card book, how should the expected-loss allowance be built - which balances need a reserve and which do not, how should cardholders be grouped, and how do repayment assumptions drive the size of the reserve - and what would examiners specifically test?
